keyframe_review.note: 'The territory of the kingdom was defined with the establishment of the Audiencia of Guatemala' in 1543; the page lists present-day Costa Rica, Nicaragua, Honduras, El Salvador, Guatemala and Chiapas as the captaincy. No area figure on the page. Revised 2026-10-19 after review: Petén is subtracted until 1696, because the Itza kingdom of Nojpetén and the other Maya kingdoms of central Petén stayed independent until 'Nojpetén fell to a Spanish assault on 13 March 1697' (Spanish conquest of Petén; the itza-mayans dossier ends on that date). The Caribbean coasts (Mosquito Coast, Belize) were never effectively held; the Belize logwood settlement is not drawn here: fx-46 R104 (3 Nov 2026) removed the 1783 occupation_start / 1821 occupation_end pair (counterpart british-colonial-empire), which the compiler read with Guatemala as the occupier of British-held Belize cells, the reverse of the page ('gave the British rights to cut logwood between the Hondo and Belize rivers' (1783), the 1786 Convention 'affirmed Spanish sovereignty'). The page does not say whether the Captaincy General of Guatemala or that of Yucatan held the Spanish claim (the infobox lists both), and the british-honduras dossier already draws the settlement (found Nov 1783, extension to the Sibun 1786). Costa Rica had its own civil and military governor; the History of Costa Rica page says 'The Spanish conquest of Costa Rica lasted more than half a century after it started 1510', so Costa Rica (and probably parts of Nicaragua and Honduras) is drawn from 1543 before its conquest was complete: the page dates no completion. fx-24 review (1 Nov 2026, F315): the Mosquito Coast strip (Atlántico Norte, Atlántico Sur, Gracias a Dios) is left out of this shape as it is out of ledger 1, so that ledger and keyframe agree (otherwise a 316-cell snap in 1543 and again in 1697). Mosquito Coast page: Spanish licences of 1545, 1562, 1577 and 1594 left 'no evidence' of 'even brief settlements or conquests'; 'The Spanish were unable to conquer this region during the 16th century'; 'it remained independent of outside control'; British contacts began 'around 1630'.

keyframe_review.note: From 13 March 1697 the Petén is inside the captaincy: the Spanish conquest of Petén page gives 'Nojpetén fell to a Spanish assault on 13 March 1697' and its infobox lists 'Incorporation of the Petén Basin into the Captaincy General of Guatemala'. The conquest was led by Martín de Ursúa, governor of Yucatán (New Spain), in a race with Jacinto de Barrios Leal, president of the Audiencia of Guatemala; the page gives no date or legal act for the transfer, and after the infobox the Petén is drawn with Guatemala, not with New Spain (whose dossier excludes Chiapas and Central America). The Mosquito Coast strip is still inside this shape; the decree of November 1803 takes it out (next keyframe). fx-24 (1 Nov 2026, conflict F315): now valid 1697-1787 and without the Mosquito Coast strip. Mosquito Coast page: 'The Miskito king Edward I and the British concluded a formal Treaty of Friendship and Alliance in 1740'; 'the first British appointed Superintendent in 1749-1759'; British settlement at Black River, Cape Gracias a Dios and Bluefields; Spain 'had been unable to drive the British from the coast or occupy any position'; in 1786 'Britain agreed to evacuate its settlers' and the coast was annexed to the Captaincy General only after the evacuation and the Spanish settlement of 1787. The British aggregate and the Miskito held the shore (Cliopatria draws it British 1734-1787) and Spain only claimed it.

Mosquito Coast page: in 1786 Britain agreed to evacuate its settlers; 'Beginning in 1787, around 1,200 settlers were brought in from the Iberian Peninsula' and the Spanish settled Sandy Bay, Cape Gracias a Dios and Black River (not Bluefields). Set to 1788 and not 1787 because the british-colonial-empire keyframe of 1787 still draws the shore (Cliopatria drops it in 1788), so the year of the Spanish settlers is the last year of the overlap. The strip leaves the captaincy again with the royal decree of 20 November 1803 (keyframe 1803, ledger loss).

keyframe_review.note: The Royal Decree of 20 November 1803: 'A strip along the Atlantic Ocean in Mosquito Coast was added' to the Viceroyalty of New Granada (New Granada page, which marks the claim 'citation needed'); the Mosquito Coast page says Spain 'rejected Guatemala's request on 30 November 1803' and transferred sovereignty of the coast to New Granada, a dependency of San Andrés. Neither page names the strip's boundary: the Nicaraguan North and South Atlantic regions and Gracias a Dios in Honduras are the researcher's reading. The Spanish never held the coast: the Mosquito Coast page says the Miskito drove the Spanish out on 4 September 1800 and Spanish rule was 'never restored', so the loss is a change of paper jurisdiction only.

ledger.note: 1543: the Audiencia of Guatemala fixes the kingdom's territory. 'The territory of the kingdom was defined with the establishment of the Audiencia of Guatemala'; the captaincy 'included present-day Costa Rica, Nicaragua, Honduras, El Salvador, Guatemala, and the Mexican state of Chiapas'. The page does not date the conquest of each province. Revised 2026-10-19: Petén is left out of this gain, because it stayed with the Itza kingdom until 13 March 1697 (see the 1697 gain). fx-24 (1 Nov 2026, conflict F315): the Mosquito Coast strip is left out until 1787; see the gain of 1788 and keyframe captaincy-general-of-guatemala_1788.

1609: the governor and Audiencia president also becomes captain general. 'The area became one [a captaincy general] in 1609, when the governor and Audiencia president also received the title of captain general.' No territorial change.

region.text: Petén, from the Itza kingdom of Nojpetén and the other independent Maya kingdoms of central Petén

ledger.note: 1697 (13 March): Nojpetén falls and the Petén is incorporated into the captaincy. 'Nojpetén fell to a Spanish assault on 13 March 1697', the end of the last independent Maya kingdom; the infobox lists 'Incorporation of the Petén Basin into the Captaincy General of Guatemala'. The conquest was led from Yucatán (governor Ursúa) against the Guatemalan president Barrios Leal's rival expedition; the page gives no date or legal act for the transfer to Guatemala, so the region is the infobox's reading (confidence 2).
1776: the capital moves from Antigua to Guatemala City. 'Antigua was ordered abandoned after earthquakes' in 1776 and Guatemala City became the capital.

region.text: the Mosquito Coast strip (Atlántico Norte, Atlántico Sur, Gracias a Dios): Miskito and British ground, claimed but not held by Spain before 1787

ledger.note: 1788 (settlers from 1787): the Spanish take up the Mosquito Coast after the British evacuation. Mosquito Coast page: in the 1786 Convention of London 'Britain agreed to evacuate its settlers and their slaves from the coast'; 'Beginning in 1787, around 1,200 settlers were brought in from the Iberian Peninsula', at Sandy Bay, Cape Gracias a Dios and Black River; before 1787 Spain 'had been unable to drive the British from the coast or occupy any position'. The coast stays Miskito in fact (the Miskito king's line continues on the page); the dossier carries the Spanish claim it held from 1787 to the 1803 decree, as the 1803 loss to New Granada expects. Dated 1788 so that it follows the last year in which the british-colonial-empire shape still draws the shore.

ledger.note: 1803 (20 November): a royal decree gives New Granada a strip of the Mosquito Coast. 'A strip along the Atlantic Ocean in Mosquito Coast was added by the Royal Decree of 20 November 1803' (the page's claim carries a 'citation needed' tag); the Mosquito Coast page dates the Spanish government's refusal of Guatemala's request to 30 November 1803. The year and month are the page's; the strip's land is the researcher's reading. The Spanish had been driven off the coast in 1800: the loss is on paper only. Mirrors viceroyalty-of-new-granada /ledger gain of 1803-11.

notes:
Written by am-06-x from two pages (budget 2-5). Not settled:
(1) The page gives the 1527 establishment and the 1543 definition of the territory but no area, and no date for the conquest of any province (Chiapas, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica); the 1543 shape is the page's list of modern countries, so Costa Rica and Nicaragua are drawn 1543-1821 although Spanish control there came later and the Caribbean coast was never held.
(2) Relation to New Spain: the page says the captaincy was 'under the viceroyalty of New Spain in Central America'; the New Spain page (viceroyalty-of-new-spain dossier) says it had 'a certain level of autonomy'. Drawn as its own colony, with New Spain excluding Chiapas and Central America.
(3) The page does not cover Soconusco, the Mosquito Coast, the Treaty of Paris 1763, the 1779 attack, the 1798 battle, Panama, or the date of the 1822 annexation; the capital coordinates are the researcher's (Ciudad Vieja, Antigua, Guatemala City). Months of the capital moves are not given.
(4) 1821-1822: between the Act of Independence (15 September 1821) and the annexation by the Mexican Empire the page names no state; the dossier ends in 1821. The Cortes of Cadiz provinces (Guatemala; Nicaragua y Costa Rica; 1812-1814 and 1820-1821) and the 1786 intendancies (San Salvador, Ciudad Real, Comayagua, Leon) change administration, not borders.
(5) Counterpart british-colonial-empire is Cliopatria's British Colonial Empire row (1706-1999, group eu-11); the Baymen settlement is its occupation of Spanish land, hatched on the Spanish side.

Revision of 2026-10-19 (after the adversarial review, four more pages opened: Spanish conquest of Petén, Viceroyalty of New Granada, Mosquito Coast, History of Costa Rica):
(6) Petén: the 1543 shape no longer draws the Itza kingdom. Petén is subtracted for 1543-1696 and comes in with a 1697-3 gain from itza-mayans (fall of Nojpetén, 13 March 1697). The conquest came from Yucatán under Ursúa, but the Spanish conquest of Petén infobox lists the 'Incorporation of the Petén Basin into the Captaincy General of Guatemala', and the New Spain dossier excludes Central America, so Petén is Guatemala's; the page gives no date or act for the transfer itself (confidence 2).
(7) Mosquito Coast: a 1803-11 loss to viceroyalty-of-new-granada mirrors New Granada's gain, and the 1803 keyframe leaves the strip out. The two pages give different days for the decree (20 November on the New Granada page, 30 November on the Mosquito Coast page); the strip's land is the researcher's reading; the Spanish had been expelled in 1800 and never returned, so the loss is on paper.
(8) Costa Rica, Nicaragua, Honduras: still drawn from 1543. The History of Costa Rica page says the conquest 'lasted more than half a century after it started 1510' and gives no completion date; the Spanish conquest of Costa Rica page did not load (url_not_found, retried once). A gap-filler may still delay Costa Rica to the 1560s on a page that dates it.
